content: The systematic search focused on diagnostic accuracy and combined terms related to contact and diagnostics. This search identified only six studies. To supplement this, additional citations from Q1a were reviewed for relevance. A total of 573 citations were scanned, but only three full-text articles met the eligibility criteria for review. A PRISMA flow diagram was used to illustrate the process. Ultimately, only three studies satisfied the inclusion criteria, all of which involved at least one year of follow-up. The included studies were cohort studies that classified healthy leprosy contacts at baseline based on anti-PGL-I positivity. These studies utilized ELISA for anti-PGL-I-O-BSA positivity as a risk marker for leprosy development among contacts. One systematic review of nine studies with at least one year of follow-up on ELISA for anti-PGL-I-O-BSA showed a median sensitivity of 26% (range: 2–39%) and a median specificity of 89% (range: 83–98%). The limitations of these findings include the relatively small number of studies assessing the utility of diagnostic tests for predicting leprosy among contacts. Methodological shortcomings were noted, such as high attrition rates and the lack of blinding of outcome assessors to diagnostic test results. The systematic search identified 270 citations from Medline and 302 from Embase. Only three full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and three studies were included in the review. These included one systematic review and two primary studies, with an additional study obtained by directly approaching an author. The study by de Souza et al. (2014) was conducted in a hyperendemic area in Paraíba, Brazil. It evaluated the utility of recombinant proteins LID-1 and PADL for screening Mycobacterium leprae infection and leprosy. Seropositive individuals and a random subset of seronegative individuals underwent dermatological examination. Diagnosis was based on hypopigmented, anesthetic lesions, slit-skin smears (SSS), and examination by a leprology specialist. If there was any doubt, confirmation was done via biopsy and further review. The tests demonstrated high sensitivity (89% and 87%) for confirming diagnosis among cases but had low specificity (42% and 39%). The study by Sinha et al. (2004) assessed the utility of serodiagnostic tests for leprosy in an endemic population in South India. It considered PGL1-O-BSA and 35kDa antigens. The study population included leprosy patients, doubtful cases, and individuals without leprosy among household contacts and neighbors. The tests showed high sensitivity but low specificity, indicating their limited utility in distinguishing true cases from non-cases. The evidence summary for ELISA for anti-PGL-I in identifying contacts who develop leprosy showed moderate quality with serious inconsistency. The median sensitivity was 26% (range: 2–39%), and the median specificity was 89% (range: 83–98%). Regarding the PICO question on whether a single uniform treatment regimen for all leprosy cases is as effective and safe as the currently recommended separate regimens for multibacillary (MB) and paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, a systematic literature search was conducted. The search included studies published between 1996 and January 2017, with no language restrictions. The uniform multidrug therapy (U-MDT) regimen consisted of a single six-month regimen for both MB and PB leprosy, using rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine. The current regular regimen (R-MDT) involves 12 months of three drugs for MB leprosy and six months of two drugs for PB leprosy. The systematic search identified 34 citations, from which 16 full-text articles were retrieved. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, and non-randomized controlled trials. The studies compared U-MDT with R-MDT in terms of clinical, histological, and bacteriological improvement or cure, as well as relapse, leprosy reactions, adverse effects, feasibility, acceptability, and costs. The quality of the included studies was moderate to high risk of bias. Meta-analysis was not conducted due to the low quality of studies and serious imprecision. Evidence synthesis followed the WHO/GRADE approach, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. The results showed no significant difference in relapse rates, leprosy reactions, disability progression, or the rate of decrease in bacteriological index between U-MDT and R-MDT. However, U-MDT was associated with a higher likelihood of being smear-positive at 12 months in initially smear-negative and low bacteriological index groups, with no differences observed at longer follow-up. The limitations of the review include the use of only two bibliographic databases and the identification of very few RCTs. Serious imprecision was noted in some estimates, and the overall quality of evidence was low to moderate.
